extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (and advanced undergraduates) learning algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea'
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and basic properties of the blow-up of a subscheme X in a scheme Y (exceptional divisor, transforms, existence via Proj/Rees algebra, behavior under regular embeddings, examples and computations). Includes exercises and lemmas for computing and using blow-ups to resolve singularities and base loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of blow-up (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bl_X Y is given by a Cartesian diagram with map β: Bl_X Y → Y such that EXY (the scheme-theoretic pullback of X by β) is an effective Cartier divisor on Bl_X Y, and for any other Cartesian diagram W → Y with D an effective Cartier divisor on W the diagram factors uniquely through Bl_X Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universal property uniquely determines the blow-up up to unique isomorphism. The formulation as a final object in the category of such squares is emphasized (Yoneda-style argument). Alternate terminology: monoidal transformation, σ-process, quadratic transformation; EXY is called the exceptional divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total transform and proper (strict) transform
rubrics_metrics.description:
If Z ⊂ Y is a closed subscheme then β^{-1}Z is the total transform of Z. The proper (or strict) transform is β^{-1}(Z - X) (scheme-theoretic closure of the preimage of Z 
ot
i X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper transform is naturally isomorphic to Bl_{X∩Z} Z in the closed-embedding case (Blow-up Closure Lemma 22.2.6). The text uses 'proper transform' terminology and later gives a more general definition; expect to compute proper transforms via closures in the blow-up of ambient spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up is isomorphism away from the center
rubrics_metrics.description: β|_{Bl_X Y - EXY} : Bl_X Y - EXY → Y - X is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 22.2.2: the blow-up does not change Y outside the locus being blown up; this is useful for local computations and for arguments reducing to checking properties on EXY.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial and extreme cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is empty then Bl_X Y = Y. If X is an effective Cartier divisor then the blow-up is an isomorphism. If X = Y then Bl_X Y = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.A and Observation 22.2.1 give these checks of the universal property in trivial cases; they are sanity checks and help avoid pathological confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization and gluing of blow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Blow-ups can be computed locally: for U an open subset of Y, Bl_{X∩U} U ≅ β^{-1}(U). If Y is covered by opens Y_α and each Bl_{X∩Y_α} Y_α exists, then Bl_X Y exists and is obtained by gluing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.B: existence and computations reduce to checking afﬁne/local pieces; this justifies many explicit affine constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence for locally principal closed subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is locally cut out by one equation (locally principal), then the blow-up Bl_X Y exists (reduce to affine case Spec A/(t)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.2.4 works through the affine ring-theoretic argument (showing φ(t) is not a zero-divisor etc.). Useful geometric interpretation: Spec A/I inside Spec A can be seen as 'shaving off fuzz supported in V(t)'. Exercises 22.2.D–F guide checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up Closure Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fibered square with closed embeddings (finite type ideal sheaves) W → Z → Y and the blow-up β: Bl_X Y → Y, taking base change and scheme-theoretic closure yields (Bl_W Z, E_{WZ}) canonically isomorphic to (Z, E_Z): in words, the proper transform of Z in Bl_X Y is the blow-up of Z along W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 22.2.6 is central for computing blow-ups: it allows one to compute the blow-up of a subscheme by first blowing up an ambient space and then taking closures. Exercises 22.2.E/F and the 'tricky exercise' 22.2.G guide the proof by universal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj/Rees algebra construction (existence and projectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is cut out by a finite type quasicoherent ideal sheaf I, then Bl_X Y = Proj_Y(⊕_{n≥0} I^n) (the Rees algebra). This construction satisfies the universal property of the blow-up and the blow-up morphism is projective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.2 and §22.3 show two approaches: explicit embedding/relations (Approach 1) or the Proj construction (Approach 2). Because the graded algebra is generated in degree 1 and finite type, Hypotheses 17.2.1 apply to get Proj as a projective Y-scheme. Projectivity implies quasicompact, proper, finite type, separated; hence blow-up preserves many finiteness properties (and for k-varieties gives k-varieties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor corresponds to O(1) on Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Proj construction Bl_X Y = Proj_Y(⊕ I^n), the preimage of X corresponds to the invertible sheaf O(1) on this Proj; the exceptional divisor EXY is the effective Cartier divisor in the class of O(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The graded module with degree shift interpretation shows the pullback of X is an effective Cartier divisor and identifies the invertible sheaf. Formula (22.3.2.1) gives EXY as Proj_X(⊕ I^n/I^{n+1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit affine equations for blow-up (computational approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach 1: when X = V(f1,...,fn) in an affine Spec A, Bl_X Y can be realized as the locus in Spec A × Proj k[X1,...,Xn] cut out by the relations x_i X_j − x_j X_i = 0 (or by pulling back Bl_{V(x1,...,xn)} Spec Z[x1,...,xn] and taking closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives concrete coordinate patches (e.g., for blowing up A^2 at the origin one gets Proj k[x,y,X,Y] with relation xY − yX = 0, and two affine patches yielding explicit smooth charts). Useful for computations and examples (Exercises in §22.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor as Proj over the center (concrete description)
rubrics_metrics.description: EXY = Proj_X(⊕_{n≥0} I^n/I^{n+1}) (viewed as a Proj over X), describing the exceptional divisor as projectivized normal cone when X is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description motivates the definition of the normal cone and connects the exceptional divisor to the projectivized normal cone/bundle in good cases (regular embeddings). See 22.3.6 and subsequent exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal cone and tangent cone
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is cut out by I in Y, then the normal cone N_{X}Y := Spec_X(⊕_{n≥0} I^n/I^{n+1}). For X a closed point p, this is the tangent cone to Y at p; the projectivized tangent cone is EXY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The normal cone is an algebro-geometric 'tubular neighborhood' analogue; in smooth cases it often identifies with the total space of the normal bundle, but in general it need not embed into Y. Exercises show examples (nodal cubic, cone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior for regular embeddings (Sym^n(I/I^2) ≅ I^n/I^{n+1})
rubrics_metrics.description: If i: X ↪ Y is a regular embedding with ideal sheaf I, then the natural map Sym^n(I/I^2) → I^n/I^{n+1} is an isomorphism; consequently I^n/I^{n+1} is locally free and the normal cone is the total space of the normal bundle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.8 (proved later) and Exercise 22.3.D explain that in this case EXY is a projective bundle (the projectivized normal bundle) over X and many nice geometric descriptions follow. The proof is technical (lifting maps, using regular sequences) but yields practical computational simplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal bundle to exceptional divisor (O(−1) in regular cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal bundle to an effective Cartier divisor D is the line bundle O(D)|_D. In the blow-up of a point in the plane, the exceptional divisor has normal bundle O(−1). More generally, for a regular embedding the normal bundle to EXY restricts to O(−1) on projective-bundle fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.2.H and 22.3.5: these identifications are useful when analyzing blow-downs (e.g., Castelnuovo's Criterion) and for computing intersection-theoretic invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness: blow-up of a smooth embedding is smooth
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ↪ Y is a closed embedding of smooth varieties over a field k, then Bl_X Y is smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.10: reduce to checking smoothness at points of EXY; by regular embedding theory EXY is a projective bundle over X and an effective Cartier divisor, so slicing criterion for regularity yields smoothness. Uses earlier exercises about regular embeddings and normal bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity at a regular point and multiplicity in total transform
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is a function on a locally Noetherian scheme X, its multiplicity at a regular point p is the largest m with f in m_p^m. The multiplicity of the exceptional divisor in the total transform of a subscheme Z of A^n when blowing up the origin equals the smallest multiplicity (at the origin) of a defining equation of Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.4.7 and Exercise 22.4.J: this gives a quantitative measure of how singularities change under blow-up and is used in explicit resolution-by-blow-up computations (nodal/cuspidal examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-ups resolve base loci of linear series (resolve rational maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an invertible sheaf L on Y with sections s_0,...,s_n whose base locus is X, the rational map Y ↠ P^n extends uniquely to a morphism Bl_X Y → P^n; the corresponding invertible sheaf is (β^* L)(−EXY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.4.L: blowing up the base locus removes base points because EXY is an effective Cartier divisor (a non-zero-divisor locally) so one can 'divide out' the common vanishing to obtain a base-point-free linear series. This is the standard way to resolve rational maps to projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-ups used for resolving singularities (strategy and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequential blowing up of singular loci (usually regular subvarieties inside the singular locus) can resolve varieties in characteristic 0 (Hironaka). Examples: blowing up plane curve singularities (nodes, cusps), A_n surface singularities, cone resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.4 gives numerous exercises (22.4.B–22.4.F, G–I) working through explicit desingularizations; 22.4.6 remarks on Hironaka's theorem and limitations in positive characteristic. Use Blow-up Closure Lemma and multiplicity considerations to plan sequences of blow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational patch description (charts) for blow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: In concrete examples (e.g., Bl_{(0,0)} A^2), the blow-up can be covered by affine charts obtained from Proj coordinates: e.g., for A^2 with coords x,y, Bl = Proj k[x,y,X,Y] with relation xY − yX = 0; charts [X,Y]=[s,1] and [1,t] yield affine pieces Spec k[y,s] and Spec k[x,t].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.4.1 demonstrates how to read off the exceptional divisor in each chart (cut out by y or x in respective charts). This method is practical for checking smoothness and computing intersections of proper transforms with EXY.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up of nonreduced centers can introduce singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up a nonreduced subscheme of a regular scheme can produce singularities (example: blow up V(y, x^2) in Spec k[x,y] yields an A_1 surface singularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.4.G warns that the center being nonreduced or having embedded components can complicate the outcome; thus choose centers carefully when attempting desingularization.
